fichas.title: Warehousing
fichas.summary: Warehousing connects production and marketing within the material-flow process. The page classifies static and dynamic storage systems, illustrates storage arrangements within production, compares centralised and decentralised storage, and gives basic warehouse traffic, aisle, and rack-height dimensions.
uses: Store raw materials, consumables, bought-in parts, intermediate production, and finished goods
Buffer the flow between market and production
Support goods movement and order fulfilment

Warehousing

Basics
Storage is part of the material flow process and logistically forms
the connection between production and marketing --7 0. Storage
is cost-intensive and does not create economic value, leading to
attempts to minimise the storage quantities and times or effectively combine the storage and transport of materials and goods
through flexible 'just-in-time production'.

There is a wide range of different static and dynamic storage
systems available for each storage situation and the goods needing storage --7 f). The spatial arrangement of the different warehouses in the production process can also be dealt with in various
ways --7 e.

Picking
Picking, or order assembly, denotes collecting articles out of the
warehouse and making them ready for dispatch in accordance
with an order. This can be single-stage picking (specific to one
order) or two-stage picking, with an intermediate picking zone for
temporary storage and assignment of the articles to a number of
orders.

fichas.title: Picking and Order Assembly
fichas.summary: Picking collects articles from the warehouse and prepares them for dispatch against an order. It may be single-stage or two-stage, with an intermediate picking zone for temporary storage and allocation. Systems range from manual, one-dimensional man-to-goods picking to systems with automated transport and goods-to-man operation.
uses: Collect articles from storage for an order
Temporarily store and allocate articles among orders
